source_text: Ixiup autem, quod ait: Quoties volui colligere filios tuos, et nolwisti ? veterem legem libertatis hominis manifestavit, quia liberum eum Deus fecit ab initio, habentem suam potestatem, sicut et suam animam, ad utendum sententia Dei voluntarie, et non coactum a Deo. Vis enim a Deo non fit, sed bona sententia adest illi semper. Et propter hoe consilium° quidem bonum dat omnibus. Posuit autem in homine potestatem electionis, quemadmodum et in angelis: (etenim angeli rationabiles:) uti hi quidem qui obedissent juste bonum sint possidentes, datum quidem a Deo, servatum vero ab ipsis. Qui autem non obedierunt, juste non inyenientur cum bono, et meritam pcenam percipient: quoniam Deus quidem dedit benigne bonum, ipsi vero non custodierunt diligenter illud, neque pretiosum arbitrati sunt, sed supereminentiam bonitatis contemserunt. Abjicientes igitur bonum et quasi respuentes, merito omnes justum judicium incident Dei, quemadmodum et Apostolus Paulus in ea epistola quze est ad Romanos, testificatus est, dicens ita: An divitias bonitatis ejus, et patientia, et longanimitatis contemnis, ignorans quoniam bonitas Dei \in poenitentiam te Secundwm autem duritiam tuam et cor imponitens saurisas tibimetipsi tram in diem ire et revelationis justi judicit Dei. Gloria autem et honor, inquit, omni operanti bonum. Dedit ergo Deus bonum, quemadmodum et Apostolus testificatur in eadem epistola, et qui operantur quidem illud, gloriam et honorem percipient, quoniam operati sunt bonum cum possint non operari illud ; hi autem qui illud non operantur, judicium justum excipient quoniam non sunt operati bonum cum possint operari illud. Ostensio quod non natura quidam boni sint, quidam vero mali, sed quod in hominis electione sit bonum. 1. Sr autem naturaliter quidam boni, quidam vero mali facti fuissent ; neque hi laudabiles essent qui boni sunt, tales enim facti fuerant, sed neque illi vituperabiles, et ipsi enim tales fuerant instituti. Sed quoniam omnes ejusdem sunt nature, et potentes retinere et operari bonum, et potentes rursum amittere id et non facere; juste etiam apud homines sensatos (quanto magis apud Deum) alii quidem laudantur, et dignum percipiunt testimonium electionis bonze et perseverantize ; alii vero accusantur, et dignum percipiunt damnum, eo quod justum et bonum reprobaverint. Et ideo prophetee bonum quidem hortabantur homines, justitiam agere bonumque operari, sicut per multa ostendimus: quia in nobis sit hoc, et propter multam negligentiam in oblivionem inciderimus, et consilio egeamus bono: propter quod bonus Deus bonum consilium per prophetas. Propter hoe autem et Dominus, Luceat lumen vestrum, dicebat, coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et clarificent Patrem vestrum qui in caelis Et: Attendite vobis, ne forte graventur corda vestra in crapula, et ebrietate, et sollicitudinibus secularibus. Et: Sint lumbi vestri preecincti, et lucerne ardentes, et vos similes hominibus exspectantibus Dominum suum, quando revertatur a nuptiis, ut cum et pulsaverit aperiant ei. Beatus servus ille, quem, cum venerit Dominus ejus, invenerit ita facientem. Et iterum: Servus qui scit voluntatem Domini sui, et non facit, vapulabit >multas. Et: Quid mihi dicitis, Domine, Domine, et non facitis que dico? Et iterum: Si autem dicat serous in corde suo, Tardat Dominus, et caedere conservos, et manducare et bibere et inebriari, veniet Dominus ejus in die qua non sperat, et dividet ewm, et partem ejus cum hypocritis ponet. Et omnia talia quee liberum et suze potestatis ostendunt hominem, et quia consilio instruat Deus, adhortans nos ad subjectionem sibi, et avertens ab incredulitate, non tamen de violentia cogens. 2. Etenim ipsum Evangelium si noluerit quis sequi, licet quidem ei, non tamen expedit. Inobedientia enim Dei et amissio boni est quidem in hominis potestate; leesionem autem et damnum non quamlibet infert. Et propter hoc Paulus ait: Omnia licent, sed non omnia expediunt; et libertatem referens hominis, quapropter et omnia licent, non cogente eum Deo; et id,non expedit, ostendens, ut non ad velamen malitiz abutamur libertate: non enim hoe expedit. Et iterum ait: Loguimini veritatem wnusquisexeat, aut turpitudo, aut vaniloquium, aut scurrilitas, que ad rem pertinent, sed magis gratiarum actio. Et: Hratis enim alitenebree, nunc autem lumen in Domino: quasi filii lucis ambulate: non in comessationibus, et ebrietatibus, non in cubilibus, et in libidinibus, non in ira, et zelo. Et hec ®quidam Suistis, sed abluti estis, sed sanctijicati estis in nomine Domini nostri. Si igitur non in nobis esset facere hee, aut non facere, quam causam habebat Apostolus, et multo prius ipse Dominus, consilium dare, queedam’ quidem facere, a quibusdam’ vero abstinere ? Sed quoniam liberze sententize ab initio est homo, et liberze sententize est Deus cujus ad similitudinem factus est, semper consilium datur ei continere bonum, quod perficitur ex ea que est ad Deum obedientia. Et non tantum in operibus, sed etiam in fide, liberum et suze potestatis arbitrium hominis servavit Dominus, Secundum fidem tuam fiat tibi; propriam fidem hominis ostendens, quoniam propriam suam habet sententiam. Et iterum: Omnia possibilia credenti; et, Vade, sicut credidisti, fiat tibi. Et omnia talia suze potestatis secundum fidem ostendunt hominem. Et propter hoc, is qui credit et habet vitam cwternam: qui autem credit Filio, non thabet vitam ceternam, sed ira Dei manebit super ipsum. Secundum hance igitur rationem, et suum proprium bonum ostendens Dominus, et sui arbitrii ac suze potestatis hominem significans, dicebat ad Hierusalem: Quoties volui * congregare Jilios tuos, quemadmodum gallina pullos suos sub ®ascellas et nolwisti? Quapropter relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta. 1. Qui autem his contraria dicunt, ipsi impotentem introducunt Dominum, scilicet quasi non potuerit perficere hoc quod Voluerit: aut rursum ignorantem natura choicos, ut ipsi dicunt, et eos qui non possunt accipere ejus incorruptelam. Sed oportebat, inquit, eum neque angelos tales fecisse, ut possent transgredi, neque homines qui statim ingrati exsisterent in eum, quoniam rationabiles et examinatores et judiciales facti sunt, et non quemadmodum irrationabilia sive inanimalia, quee sua voluntate nihil possunt agere, sed cum necessitate et vi ad bonum trahuntur, quibus unus sensus et unus mos, inflexibiles et sine judicio, qui nihil aliud esse possunt, preeterquam quod facti sunt. Sic autem nec suave esset eis, quod est bonum, neque pretiosa communicatio Dei, neque magnopere appetendum bonum, quod sine suo proprio motu et cura et studio provenisset, sed ultro et otiose insitum : ut essent nullius momenti boni, eo quod natura magis quam voluntate tales exsisterent, et ultroneum haberent bonum, sed non secundum electionem; et propter hoc nec hoc ipsum intelligentes, quoniam pulchrum sit quod bonum, neque fruentes eo. Quze enim fruitio boni apud eos qui ignorant? Quze autem gloria his qui non illud? Quee autem corona his qui non eam, ut victores in certamine, consecuti sunt? Et propter hoc Dominus violentum dixit regnum coelorum : e¢ gui vim faciunt, inquit, diripiunt illud ; hoc est, qui cum vi et agone vigilantes instanter diripiunt illud. Propter hoe autem et Paulus Apostolus ait Corinthiis: Nescitis, quoniam hi qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidem currunt, sed unus accipit bravium. Sic currite, ut apprehendatis. Omnis autem qui agonisatur, in omnibus continens est: ili quidem ut corruptibilem accipiant coronam, nos autem incorruptibilem. Ego autem sic curro, non in incertum: sic pugno, non quasi aérem cewsed lividum facio corpus meum, et in servitutem redigo, ne Sorte aliis preedicans, ipse reprobus efficiar. Bonus igitur agonista ad incorruptele agonem adhortatur nos, uti coronemur, et pretiosam arbitremur coronam, videlicet que per agonem nobis acquiritur, sed non ultro coalitam. Et quanto per agonem nobis advenit, tanto est pretiosior: quanto autem pretiosior, tanto eam semper diligamus. Sed neque similiter diliguntur ea que ultro adveniunt, quam illa que cum multa sollicitudine adinveniuntur. Quoniam igitur pro nobis erat, plus diligere Deum, cum agone hoe nobis adinvenire, et Dominus docuit, et Apostolus tradidit. Et alias autem esset videlicet nostrum insensatum bonum, quod Tesset inexercitatum. Sed et videre non tantum nobis esset desiderabile, nisi cognovissemus quantum esset malum non videre: et bene valere autem male valentis experientia honorabilius efficit; et lucem, tenebrarum comparatio; et vitam, mortis. Sic et cceleste honorabilius est his qui cognoverunt terrenum. Quanto autem honorabilius, tanto magis diligimus illud; et si plus illud dilexerimus, clariores erimus apud Deum. 2. Pro nobis igitur omnia hee sustinuit Dominus, uti per omnia eruditi, in omnibus in futurum simus cauti, et perseveremus in omni ejus dilectione, rationabiliter edocti diligere Deum: Deo quidem magnanimitatem preestante in apostasia hominis ; homine autem erudito per eam, quemadmodum et propheta ait: Himendabit te abscessio tua ; preefiniente Deo omnia ad hominis perfectionem, et ad edificationem, et manifestationem dispositionum; uti et bonitas ostendatur, et justitia perficiatur, et Ecclesia ad figuram imaginis Filii ejus coaptetur, et tandem aliquando maturus fiat homo, in tantis maturescens ad videndum et capiendum Deum.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed, what He says: How often I wanted to gather your sons, and you did not want to, He manifested the old law of the freedom of man, because God made him free from the beginning, having his own power, just as he has his own soul, to use the sentence of God voluntarily, and not being forced by God. For power is not done by God, but good sentence is always present to him. And because of this, He gives good counsel to all. But He put in man the power of election, just as in angels, for angels are rational. So that those who obeyed would justly possess good, given by God, but preserved by themselves. But those who did not obey would not justly find good, and would receive the penalty they deserved, because God gave good kindly, but they did not keep it carefully, nor did they consider it precious, but they despised the superiority of goodness. Therefore, throwing away good and as if spurning it, all justly incur the judgment of God, just as Apostle Paul testified in that epistle which is to the Romans, saying: Do you despise the riches of His goodness and patience and long-suffering, ignoring that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But to those who are hard-hearted and obstinate, He will render according to their deeds. For glory and honor are to everyone who does good. Therefore, God gave good, just as Apostle Paul testifies in the same epistle, and those who do good will receive glory and honor, because they did good when they could not do it; but those who do not do good will receive just judgment, because they did not do good when they could do it. This shows that some are not good by nature, and some are not evil, but that good is in the election of man. For if some were naturally good, and some were naturally evil, neither those who are good would be praiseworthy, because they were made such, nor would those who are evil be blameworthy, because they were instituted such. But because all are of the same nature, and able to retain and do good, and able again to lose it and not do it, justly also among sensible men, and much more before God, some are praised and receive worthy testimony of good election and perseverance, and others are accused and receive worthy loss, because they rejected just and good things. And therefore, prophets exhorted men to do justice and work good, as we show through many things, because it is in us to do this, and because of much negligence we have fallen into oblivion, and we need good counsel, for which good God gives good counsel through prophets. And for this reason, the Lord said: Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven. And: Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down in carousing and drunkenness and worldly cares. And: Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning, and you like men waiting for their Lord, when he returns from the wedding, that when he knocks, they may open to him. Blessed is that servant, whom when his Lord comes, he finds doing so. And again: The servant who knows the will of his Lord and does not do it will be beaten much. And: Why do you say to me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say? And again: If the servant says in his heart, My Lord delays, and begins to beat his fellow servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the Lord will come on a day when he does not expect, and will cut him off, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites. And all such things show that man is free and of his own power, and that God instructs us with counsel, exhorting us to subjection to Him, and turning us away from unbelief, not however compelling us with violence. For if someone does not want to follow the Gospel, it is permitted to him, but it is not expedient. For disobedience to God and loss of good is in the power of man, but the lesion and damage are not inflicted in any way. And because of this, Paul says: All things are permitted, but not all things are expedient. And referring to the freedom of man, for which reason all things are permitted, not compelling him, God shows that it is not expedient to abuse liberty for malice. And again he says: Let each one speak the truth with his neighbor, or else turpitude, or vanity, or scurrility, which pertain to the matter, but rather the giving of thanks. And: For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and lusts, not in anger and zeal. And such things you did, but you were washed, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord. If therefore it were not in us to do these things or not to do them, what reason would the Apostle have had, and much earlier the Lord Himself, to give counsel, to do some things and to abstain from others? But because man is free from the beginning, and God, whose likeness he was made in, is also free, counsel is always given to him to contain good, which is perfected from obedience to God. And not only in works, but also in faith, the Lord has preserved the free and voluntary judgment of man, saying: According to your faith, let it be to you, showing the proper faith of man, because he has his own sentence. And again: All things are possible to him who believes; and: Go, as you have believed, so it will be to you. And all such things show that man is of his own power according to faith. And because of this, he who believes and has eternal life, but he who believes in the Son does not have eternal life, but the wrath of God remains on him. According to this reason, the Lord shows His own proper good and signifies man of his own judgment and his own power, saying to Jerusalem: How often I wanted to gather your sons, as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings, and you did not want to? Therefore, your house will be left to you desolate. But those who say the opposite introduce an impotent Lord, as if He could not perfect what He wanted, or else ignorant of the nature of choices, as they say, and of those who cannot receive His incorruptibility. But it was necessary for Him not to make angels such that they could transgress, nor men who would immediately be ungrateful to Him, because they were made rational and examiners and judicial, and not like irrational or inanimate things, which can do nothing by their own will, but are drawn to good by necessity and force, having one sense and one custom, inflexible and without judgment, which can be nothing other than what they were made. For it would not be sweet to them what is good, nor precious the communication of God, nor greatly desirable the good that would come without their own motion and care and study, but rather would be instilled in them without effort and idly, so that they would be of no moment, because they would exist more by nature than by will, and would have good not by election, but by nature; and because of this, they would not even understand that what is good is beautiful, nor would they enjoy it. For what enjoyment of good is there among those who are ignorant? What glory is there for those who do not have it? What crown is there for those who have not obtained it, as victors in a contest? And because of this, the Lord said that the kingdom of heaven is taken by violence, saying: Those who make violence take it by force, that is, those who, with force and struggle, vigilantly and instantly seize it. And because of this, Apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: Do you not know that those who run in a stadium, all indeed run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. And every athlete exercises self-control in all things, they indeed to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible one. I so run, not in uncertainty, so I fight, not as one beating the air, but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, while preaching to others, I myself become disqualified. The good athlete exhorts us to the contest for incorruptibility, that we may be crowned, and that we may consider the crown precious, which is acquired for us through the contest, but not instilled in us without effort. And the more it comes to us through the contest, the more precious it is, and the more we always love it. But those things that come without effort are not loved in the same way as those that are found with much solicitude. Because it was for our sake that we love God more, when we acquire Him through this contest, and the Lord taught, and the Apostle handed down. And otherwise, our good would be insensible, which would be unexercised. But also, it would not be desirable for us to see, unless we knew how great the evil is of not seeing, and to be well is more honorable through the experience of being ill, and light is more honorable through the comparison with darkness, and life is more honorable through death. So also, the heavenly is more honorable to those who have known the earthly. The more honorable it is, the more we love it, and if we love it more, we will be more glorious before God. Therefore, the Lord suffered all these things for our sake, that through all things we may be instructed, and in the future we may be cautious in all things, and persevere in all His love, rationally taught to love God, God indeed showing magnanimity in the apostasy of man, but man being instructed through it, as the prophet says: Your departure will instruct you. God predestining all things for the perfection of man, and for edification, and for the manifestation of His dispositions, that His goodness may be shown, and His justice may be perfected, and the Church may be conformed to the figure of the image of His Son, and finally, man may become mature, maturing in so many things to see and grasp God.

pass_b_english: Indeed, the very words He speaks reveal the ancient law of human freedom: "How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing?" (Matt 23:37). God made humanity free from the beginning, possessing a power of its own, just as it possesses its own soul, so that it might use God's judgment voluntarily and not be forced by God. For coercion does not come from God; rather, a good judgment is always present to us. And for this reason He gives good counsel to all. He placed the power of choice in man, just as He did in angels — for angels are rational — so that those who obeyed would justly possess the good, given by God but preserved by themselves. Those who did not obey, however, would not justly find the good and would receive the penalty they deserved, since God gave the good generously, but they did not guard it carefully, nor consider it precious, but despised the surpassing excellence of His goodness. Thus, casting aside the good and virtually spurning it, all justly incur the judgment of God, just as the Apostle Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Romans: "Do you despise the riches of His kindness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God" (Rom 2:4–5). "Glory and honor," he says, "to everyone who does good" (Rom 2:10). Therefore God gave the good, as the Apostle attests in that same letter; those who work it receive glory and honor because they did good when they could have refrained, while those who do not work it receive just judgment because they failed to do good when they could have done it.

This demonstrates that no one is good by nature and no one evil by nature, but that goodness lies in human election. If some were naturally good and others naturally evil, the good would not be praiseworthy — for they were made so — nor the evil blameworthy — for they were constituted so. But because all share the same nature, capable both of retaining and doing good and of losing it and not doing it, it is just — among sensible men, how much more before God — that some are praised and receive worthy testimony for their good election and perseverance, while others are accused and suffer deserved loss because they rejected what is just and good. For this reason the prophets exhorted men to practice justice and do good, as we have shown in many passages: because this capacity resides in us, and through much negligence we have fallen into oblivion and need good counsel. Therefore the good God gives good counsel through the prophets. And for this reason the Lord said, "Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven" (Matt 5:16). And: "Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of this life" (Luke 21:34). And: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like men waiting for their master to return from the wedding feast, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him at once" (Luke 12:35–36). Blessed is that servant whom his master finds so doing when he comes. And again: "The servant who knows his master's will but does not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating" (Luke 12:47). And: "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?" (Luke 6:46). And again: "If that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed in coming,' and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful" (Luke 12:45–46). All such passages show that man is free and possesses his own power, and that God instructs us by counsel, exhorting us to submit to Him and turning us from unbelief, yet not compelling us by violence.

For even the Gospel itself — if anyone does not wish to follow it, it is permitted to him, but it is not expedient. Disobedience to God and the loss of the good are indeed within man's power, but the injury and damage are not inflicted in just any way. Because of this Paul says: "All things are lawful, but not all things are helpful" (1 Cor 6:12; 10:23), and by referring to the freedom of man — for which reason all things are lawful, God not compelling him — he shows that it is not helpful to use liberty as a cover for malice; that is not expedient. And again he says: "Let each one speak the truth with his neighbor" (Eph 4:25), putting away falsehood, foul talk, empty words, and jesting, which are not fitting, but rather giving of thanks (Eph 5:4). And: "For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light" (Eph 5:8) — not in revelries and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. "And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Cor 6:11). If it were not in our power to do these things or refrain from them, what reason would the Apostle have had — and much earlier the Lord Himself — to give counsel, commanding some things and forbidding others? But because man is free from the beginning, and God — in whose likeness he was made — is also free, counsel is always given to him to hold fast to the good, which is perfected through obedience to God.

And not only in works, but also in faith, the Lord has preserved the free and voluntary judgment of man, saying: "According to your faith let it be done to you" (Matt 9:29), showing the proper faith of man, because he has his own judgment. And again: "All things are possible for one who believes" (Mark 9:23); and: "Go your way; as you have believed, so let it be done for you" (Matt 8:13). All such passages show that man acts by his own power according to faith. And because of this, "whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36). According to this same reasoning, the Lord displayed His own proper good and signified man as possessing his own judgment and power, saying to Jerusalem: "How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing? Behold, your house is left to you desolate" (Matt 23:37–38). Those who teach the opposite introduce an impotent Lord — as if He could not accomplish what He willed — or else a Lord ignorant of the nature of choices, as they say, and of those who cannot receive His incorruptibility. But it was necessary that He not make angels such that they could transgress, nor men who would immediately prove ungrateful to Him; for they were made rational, examiners, and judges, unlike irrational or inanimate things which can do nothing by their own will but are drawn to the good by necessity and force, having one sense and one fixed habit, inflexible and without judgment, incapable of being anything other than what they were made.

For it would not be sweet to them what is good, nor would the communion of God be precious, nor would the good be greatly desired if it came without their own motion, care, and study, but were instead implanted in them effortlessly and idly. Then the good would be of no account, because they would exist by nature rather than by will, possessing the good not by election but by nature; and for this reason they would not even understand that the good is beautiful, nor would they enjoy it. For what enjoyment of the good is there among those who are ignorant? What glory for those who do not possess it? What crown for those who have not won it as victors in a contest? And for this reason the Lord said, "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force" (Matt 11:12) — that is, those who with force and struggle, watching vigilantly, seize it eagerly. And for this reason the Apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: "Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it" (1 Cor 9:24). Every athlete exercises self-control in all things; they do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one. "I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified" (1 Cor 9:26–27). The good athlete exhorts us to the contest for incorruptibility, that we may be crowned and consider the crown precious — the crown acquired for us through the contest, not implanted without effort. The more it comes to us through the contest, the more precious it is; the more precious, the more we always love it. But things that come without effort are not loved in the same way as those found with great solicitude. Because it was for our sake that we might love God more when we acquire Him through this contest, the Lord taught and the Apostle handed down. Otherwise our good would be insensible — unexercised. Nor would seeing be desirable to us unless we knew how great an evil it is not to see; health is made more honorable through the experience of sickness; light through the comparison with darkness; life through death. So also the heavenly is more honorable to those who have known the earthly. The more honorable, the more we love it; and if we love it more, we shall be more glorious before God.

Therefore the Lord endured all these things for our sake, that through all things we might be instructed, and in the future be cautious in all things, and persevere in all His love, rationally taught to love God: God indeed showing magnanimity in the apostasy of man, but man being instructed through it, as the prophet says: "Your departure will instruct you" (Jer 2:19). God predestining all things for the perfection of man, for edification, and for the manifestation of His dispositions; that His goodness may be shown, His justice perfected, the Church conformed to the image of His Son, and finally that man may become mature, maturing through so many things to see and grasp God.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the nuances of agency (e.g., 'not being forced by God' for 'non coactum a Deo') and the distinction between nature and election. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly identified and added to the text (e.g., Matt 23:37, Rom 2:4-5, 1 Cor 9:24) as required by the instructions. The title 'Human Freedom and God's Goodness' captures the central thought of the chapter.

source: Ixiup autem, quod ait: Quoties volui colligere filios tuos, et nolwisti ? veterem legem libertatis hominis manifestavit, quia liberum eum Deus fecit ab initio, habentem suam potestatem, sicut et suam animam, ad utendum sententia Dei voluntarie, et non coactum a Deo. English: But indeed, what He says: How often I wanted to gather your sons, and you did not want to, He manifested the old law of the freedom of man, because God made him free from the beginning, having his own power, just as he has his own soul, to use the sentence of God voluntarily, and not being forced by God.
